newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Property assets float planned by AMP NZ - paper.
newsitem.headline: Property assets float planned by AMP NZ - paper.

text.p: The country's largest fund manager, AMP Society, plans a property float of assets thought to be worth about NZ$500 million, the New Zealand Herald reported on Thursday.
Although in its early stages, brokers are believed to have been appointed to manage the float which could take place before the end of the year, the Herald said.
The appetite for property floats is considered to be strong.

Kiwi Income Property Trust, Shortland Property and Property For Industry have all performed well in recent months against a background of falls in long-term interest rates and expectations of rental increases.
It is likely that AMP will want to retain control of the assets, so the funds sought are not expected to be above NZ$250 million.
It was unclear whether all the property will be supplied by AMP -- another party might also be involved, the Herald said.
AMP's property fund consists of 25 properties, mainly in Auckland and Wellington. The net worth of the assets is NZ$645 million.
Its premier site is the ASB Centre in Albert Street, Auckland, in which AMP has a 40 percent holding.
Among its other downtown Auckland buildings are Quay Tower, Southpac Tower and Shortland Centre 1.
AMP also has other properties in its general fund, which could be included.
One possible issue overhanging the property float might be a decision by the law firm Russell McVeagh on its Shortland Centre lease, due to expire in 1999.
The firm is reviewing the possibility of moving to new premises and a consortium comprising AMP and Mace Developments are apparently contenders.
The consortium plans a multi-storey office building on Lion Nathan's Imperial site on the corner of Fort Street and Queen Street.

The idea of fund managers floating their property assets is not new. There were plans several years ago for institutions to band their property assets together but they foundered on the complexity of valuations and market conditions at the time.
Fund managers in Australia have moved for the past year or so to float their property assets. AMP's Australian counterpart recently listed a property vehicle.
Some of the floated Australian companies are now trading at up to 10 percent above their net tangible asset value. This premium is transparently reflected into the fund managers' retained holding.
